wine.name: Ata Rangi Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, built in large part on the Abel clone, with Dijon clones planted beside it.
wine.sites: The house's oldest Pinot Noir plantings, the home block of 1980 among them, in vineyards close around the winery on the Martinborough Terrace: shallow silt loam over deep, free draining alluvial gravel.
wine.making: Fermented with indigenous yeasts, a share of the fruit as whole bunches and the rest destemmed, for some two to three weeks on skins. The malolactic fermentation is completed in oak, and the wine spends about eleven months in French oak barrels, around a third of them new, then rests for some months after blending before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and dried herb with a savoury edge; fine boned yet firm, with the concentration of small, thick skinned berries thinned by the wind, fresh acidity and a long, fine grained finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of release, it gains savoury depth with time, and the house's own retrospectives reach back through decades of vintages.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if you like, an old one gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's name, on a label that names its grape and district and little else.

records.table: Ata Rangi Pinot Noir comes from the house's oldest vines on the Martinborough Terrace, planted from 1980 and built in large part on the Abel clone: dark cherry and dried herb, fine boned and firm. Pour it a little below room temperature in a wide glass.
records.story: In 1980 the founder bought a stony sheep paddock at the edge of Martinborough village and planted it, one of the first vineyards on a terrace that a soil survey of the late 1970s had likened to Burgundy. His first Pinot Noir cuttings came through a customs officer at Auckland. The story goes that the officer had seized a cutting smuggled into the country in a gumboot, said in the usual telling to come from Romanée-Conti, and propagated it; whatever its true source, the vine took the officer's name, Abel, and the Ata Rangi block became its mother planting, from which the clone spread across New Zealand. The founder's sister joined three years after the founding, and the first Ata Rangi Pinot Noir was released from the 1986 vintage, beside the first Célèbre, a red blend. In 1987 the founder married and his wife joined the family firm. The house added vineyards around the village over the following decades, among them a share of the Craighall vineyard, divided with Dry River in 2004. Its Pinot Noir became the bottle a sommelier opens to show what Martinborough is: savoury, firm, made from small crops thinned by the wind, and able to age.

The Abel clone, nicknamed the gumboot clone, is a New Zealand selection with its own story; it is not one of the numbered Dijon clones planted beside it.
Célèbre is the house's red blend, not a reserve Pinot Noir.

report: One secondary account gives 1985 for the first varietal Pinot Noir; the house's own page gives the first release as 1986, which the record keeps.
The Romanée-Conti origin of the Abel clone is told as legend only; a recent genotyping is reported by one source to point to a Swiss origin, so it is left out until a second source confirms it.
The customs officer who gave the clone his name is dead by the sources but his dates were not found, so he is described and only his surname stands, as the clone's name.
The founders and the family are living and never named; the vineyard count (12 or 14) and area are volatile and left out.
The library's style line (dark cherry, dried herb, firm tannin) is followed in the glass; the whole bunch share varies by vintage, so no figure is given.

wine.name: Dry River Pinot Gris
wine.grapes: Pinot Gris alone, from a small berried clone that the house traces to an import by the Mission in 1886.
wine.sites: The Dry River Estate vineyard on the Martinborough Terrace, most of the fruit from the first vines planted there in 1979, ungrafted by the house's account, in clay rich soil.
wine.making: The crop is kept very small and picked late. The fruit is fermented with its own yeasts, as is the house's rule across its whole range, and the wine is made with as little intervention as the house can manage, in its own words seeking to keep what the vineyard grew without embellishment.
wine.glass: Yellow peach, rock melon and a hint of old fashioned custard, with a savoury note of fenugreek; rich, full and textured, gently sweet in some vintages, soft in acidity, finishing dry with a trace of bitterness.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to enjoy on release, it is built, like the whole Dry River range, for long ageing, and reviewers of older vintages expect it to unfold over many years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no decanting is needed, though an older bottle opens with a little air; a white wine glass of medium size.

records.table: Dry River Pinot Gris comes from vines planted on the Martinborough Terrace in 1979, cropped very low and picked late: yellow peach, melon and a rich, textured palate, made to age. It is the bottle that shows New Zealand Pinot Gris can be a serious white.
records.story: A couple founded Dry River in 1979, planting ungrafted Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer and Sauvignon Blanc on the Martinborough Terrace, among the first vines in the district. Their first whites, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Gris and Sauvignon Blanc, were made in 1984. From the start the house kept its crops very small, picked late and made wines for the cellar rather than for early drinking. After the volcanic eruptions of 1991 cooled the seasons, the founder laid a reflective white mulch under the vines to give the fruit more light and warmth, and when summers grew hotter the house took it up again from 2014. Part of the Craighall vineyard was bought in 1997, and in 2004 the rest of it was divided between Dry River and Ata Rangi. In 2003 the founders sold the estate to new owners, among them an American investor, and the founder stayed on as winemaker; in 2022 that investor's family sold Dry River to a Wellington businessman, returning it to New Zealand hands. Through each change the Pinot Gris kept its place as the house's case for the grape: a white of weight and length from old vines on one estate, which a sommelier pours to show that New Zealand Pinot Gris need not be a simple aromatic.

report: The plan's doubt stands: the library lists the Pinot Noir first and the house is equally known for it; the Pinot Gris is kept, as the plan chose it for the group's spread, and the record can be swapped to the Pinot Noir without loss.
The vessels of fermentation and the length of time before bottling were not found for the Pinot Gris, so making says only what the house's own pages give: tiny crops, late picking and native yeasts.
The Mission import of 1886 rests on the house's own Pinot Gris page and is hedged as its account; no second source was found.
The Craighall planting is dated 1983 to 1985 by the house and 1992 by another source, so the story gives only the purchases of 1997 and 2004.
One deal register names Luna Estate as the buyer of 2022 against the NZ Herald and Bloomberg; the record follows the two news sources and names nobody.
The library calls the wine dry; tasting notes find some sweetness in some vintages and a dry finish, so the glass says so.
The founders and the buyer of 2022 are living and never named; the American investor of 2003 died in 2022 but is described, not named, to keep the line short.

wine.name: Martinborough Vineyard Home Block Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from several clones, among them the 10/5 clone of the first planting and the Abel clone.
wine.sites: The Home Block on the Martinborough Terrace, where the vineyard began in 1980, on free draining gravel; its parts include the original block of the 10/5 clone, first planted in 1980, and a block of the Abel clone.
wine.making: The fruit is picked and sorted by hand and fermented with a share of whole bunches that varies by vintage, from about a tenth to a fifth. The wine is then aged for eleven to twelve months in French oak barrels before bottling.
wine.glass: Dark cherry and ripe plum over a savoury, earthy edge of forest floor; medium bodied and supple, with fresh acidity and fine, firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous within a few years of release, it gains savoury depth over the decade that follows in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius in a wide Burgundy glass; a young bottle can take half an hour in a carafe.

records.table: Home Block Pinot Noir is Martinborough Vineyard's wine from the block where the estate began in 1980, among the district's first Pinot Noir plantings: dark cherry and plum with a savoury edge, supple and fresh. It suits duck or mushrooms.
records.story: In the late 1970s a government soil scientist studied the Wairarapa and reported that the climate and free draining soils around Martinborough resembled Burgundy's; accounts date the study to 1978 and its publication to 1979. In 1980 a group of partners founded Martinborough Vineyard on the terrace and planted the Home Block, and by the house's own account it was one of the first in the district to plant Pinot Noir and holds some of the oldest Pinot vines in New Zealand. A winemaker who joined in 1986 made the Pinot Noirs of the late 1980s and early 1990s that helped carry the district's name abroad. In 2003 the house renamed its reserve Pinot Noir Marie Zélie, and a Home Block Pinot Noir appears by the vintage of 2013. In 2014 a listed New Zealand wine company made a full takeover offer for Martinborough Vineyard Estates, and the house passed into its hands. Through those changes the Home Block has kept the estate's story: the wine from the first vines, which a sommelier pours to show where Martinborough Pinot Noir began.

The claim to have been first to plant Pinot Noir in Martinborough is the house's own and is contested (Ata Rangi planted Pinot Noir in 1980 too), so it stands only as one of the first, by the house's account.

The founders' names vary between sources and the founders and the winemaker of 1986 are living, so nobody is named; the takeover bidder of 2014 is described, not named, as its name carries a living person's.

Whole bunch shares of a tenth (2020) and a fifth (2013) come from Jancis Robinson's tasting notes as summarised in search, and the barrel time of eleven to twelve months from the house's sheets of 2019 and 2024.

The first Home Block vintage is not confirmed; the earliest found is 2013, so the story says by the vintage of 2013. The house's estate Pinot Noir and Home Block may be one wine renamed; that was not settled.

wine.name: Escarpment Kupe Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, all of it the Abel clone, by the house's account.
wine.sites: The home block on Te Muna Road, first planted in 1999, densely planted on alluvial gravel terraces at the edge of the Martinborough district.
wine.making: Fermented in open fermenters with indigenous yeasts, about half of the fruit as whole bunches in the vintages of the 2020s, hand plunged once a day for some four weeks on skins. The wine then spends about a year and a half in French oak barriques, around two fifths to a half of them new, and is bottled without fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Black cherry, wild raspberry and fruit cake with clove and pepper; dense and peppery, tight when young, with firm, slightly leathery tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and somewhat closed on release, it wants several years in bottle and then holds for a decade or more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: Decant a young bottle for an hour; serve at 15 to 17 degrees Celsius in a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Kupe is Escarpment's Pinot Noir from its close planted home block on Te Muna Road, all Abel clone, about half whole bunch and long in French oak: black cherry, fruit cake and pepper, dense and firm. Decant it young.
records.story: The founder came to Martinborough in 1986 as winemaker of Martinborough Vineyard, whose Pinot Noirs of the following years helped carry the district's name abroad. In late 1998 he and his wife, with Australian partners, bought land at 51 Te Muna Road, south east of the village, and in 1999 they planted the Escarpment vineyard as a joint venture, densely and with the Abel clone. By the house's own account Kupe began with the vintage of 2003, when a tiny crop from the low yielding home block was made into the single vineyard wine. Beside it the house made Pinot Noir from other single vineyards around the district, among them Kiwa and Pahi, and an Escarpment Pinot Noir under the house's name. In March 2018 Torbreck Vintners of the Barossa Valley announced that it would buy the business, and the purchase was completed in 2019 after the approval of New Zealand's Overseas Investment Office. Kupe is the house's flagship, and for a sommelier it shows the denser, more structured side of Martinborough Pinot Noir, a wine of whole bunches and long barrel ageing from one close planted block.

wine.name: Palliser Estate Pinot Noir
wine.sites: The house's vineyards on the Martinborough Terrace, most of the fruit from its organically farmed Hua Nui, Winery and Pencarrow vineyards, planted in 1998 and 2000.
wine.making: Hand picked fruit is cold soaked and fermented largely with wild yeasts, a small share as whole bunches in some vintages. The wine is pressed to French oak barrels and matured for about ten months, during which the malolactic fermentation takes place, before bottling.
wine.glass: Black and red cherry, raspberry and mulberry with anise, dried herb and a note of freshly mown summer hay; silky and supple on the palate, savoury and structured.
wine.ageing: Ready within a couple of years of release, it keeps and gains savoury depth for several years after that.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with a little air; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: Palliser Estate takes its name from Cape Palliser, and its Pinot Noir comes mostly from organically farmed vineyards on the Martinborough Terrace: black cherry, raspberry and dried herb, silky and savoury. Serve it a little cool in a Burgundy glass.
records.story: Palliser takes its name from Cape Palliser, the headland at the southern end of the Wairarapa, which Captain James Cook (1728 to 1779) named after a British naval officer. The business began in 1984, when the Om Santi vineyard was planted on the Martinborough Terrace; a vineyard partnership followed in 1986, and in 1988 the two were joined in the company the house became. Its first wine came from the 1989 vintage. Unlike the family estates around it, Palliser was formed as an unlisted public company held by a small number of shareholders, and it grew into one of the larger houses of the district, with Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay beside its Pinot Noir. The Hua Nui and Pencarrow vineyards were planted in 1998 and the Winery vineyard in 2000, and the house turned more of its land to organic farming, Hua Nui the first of its vineyards to gain BioGro certification. From the 2018 vintage Hua Nui was also bottled on its own. The Estate Pinot Noir, drawn mostly from those organic vineyards, is the wine a sommelier meets most often from the house: a supple, savoury Martinborough Pinot Noir that shows the district in a bottle poured widely.
